text: You're given an m by n binary matrix. An island is a group of ones connected four-directionally. The area of an island is the number of its cells. Return the maximum area, or zero if there's no island.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — it's the usual grid of land and water, but instead of how many islands there are, I want the size of the largest one. Connectivity is four-directional. Is that right?

One thing I'll note — here the grid is integers, zero and one, not characters. So I compare and write with a plain zero, no quotes. Are there any constraints on the input size? And can I modify the grid?
Up to fifty by fifty, and yes, you can modify it.
Let me run through the example. Take this small grid — a blue island of three cells and a brown island of two. The largest is three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to count islands first and then re-scan to measure each. That's two passes for no reason. This problem reminds me of flood fill, the sink-the-island pattern: each unseen land cell starts a DFS that sinks its whole island, so nothing is visited twice. The twist is that while the DFS sinks an island, I count the cells it visits. Each island's count is its area, and I keep the maximum. One pass.

Here's the plan. One: scan every cell, skipping water. Two: on land, reset a current-area counter to zero and run a DFS from there, then update the max. Three: the DFS returns on out-of-bounds or water; otherwise it sinks the cell, adds one to the counter, and recurses into four neighbors. One thing worth flagging — the counter is passed by reference. By value, each call would increment its own copy, and the top level would still see zero. An equivalent design is to have the DFS return the area as one plus the sum of its four neighbors. There's a trade-off here. Sinking mutates the grid, and a huge all-land grid could recurse deep enough to overflow — BFS would avoid that. For fifty by fifty, in-place DFS is fine. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The outer loops skip water with a continue; for each land cell I start a fresh counter at zero, run the DFS, and take the max. The DFS checks bounds and water first, sinks the cell, bumps the counter, then visits the four directions. One thing worth flagging — the counter is an int reference, so the increment inside every recursive call lands on the one counter the top level reads back. And since the grid is int, every check is against a plain zero — no quotes this time.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. The same grid, expected output three. The row that matters is the second launch. The first DFS, from the top-left corner, sank all three blue cells, so the max is already three. The scan skips those sunk cells and reaches the brown pair; its DFS counts two, and the max of three and two stays three. Return three. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. An all-water grid returns zero — DFS never launches and the max stays at its initial zero. A single land cell returns one. One solid block returns its full cell count.

The time complexity is m times n — each cell is scanned once and sunk at most once, counting as it goes. The space complexity is m times n for the recursion stack in the worst case. In the worst-case scenario, one island filling the whole grid makes the stack that deep. Oh, one more thing — this is the plain flood-fill island count with two extra lines: a current-area counter and a max. If they later asked for every island's size, I'd just push each area into a list instead of maxing.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You connected it straight to the sink-the-island pattern and measured area in the same pass. You flagged that the counter must be by reference — or the DFS must return the area — or it won't add up. And you caught that this grid is int, not char, so no quotes. Good work.
